text: And I think this is really one of the big opportunities for AI at the organizational level is that many individual people are kind of not in a position where they can change the things that are broken in an organization because no one is actually spelling it out. No one is taking a bird's eye view of looking at everything that happens in an organization and saying, hey, this over here is inefficient, this could be better, this thing keeps happening across all these different teams, but nobody's figured out that the solution has actually been discovered by that team. And these are the sorts of things that agents are great for. Agents are very capable at combing through large amounts of textual data that's unstructured and finding these kinds of patterns and turning them into something useful and surfacing them as like, okay, this workflow has a problem because it is wasting time and it's inefficient and it could be different instead. And we don't want to just do this once, though. We want this to kind of become the way that organizations adopt AI broadly where agents are able to get the context they need, but also they're able to improve both the agents themselves as well as the organizations. We want agents to be more like our coworkers, but human coworkers learn on the job. Agents currently learn on the job in relatively primitive ways, and they do this via in-context learning and ‑‑ oops, sorry. I'm going to go back a few seconds so we can edit this on the recording. Agents learn in relatively primitive ways through in‑context learning, and this typically looks like them having a skill file written by somebody or looking around a code base, but they don't get the institutional level latent knowledge that human employees really do. And so they relearn a lot, they have to rediscover things, they spend a lot of input tokens, and I think nowadays people are realizing that cached input is the bottleneck in many agent costs. And even if you do get great cash rates and cash costs go down, you still have to reprocess a lot of input to redo a workflow every single time. And so to get around this, you kind of want to be able to bake in more into the model, especially for things that are harder to write down as rules. So I like thinking about this spectrum from rules to patterns, as well as conceptually like code versus data. And so lots of things live as code and skills are kind of like this, rules are kind of like this. But things like preferences and friction, heuristics and trends, these are all data. And institutions have so much data that they are running on and the employees of the organization implicitly learn that models never really get a chance to learn. And this is the sort of thing that we see as blocking them from becoming true coworkers. And so there is a question of, like, okay, what goes in context, what goes in the weights? And part of it is you kind of need to earn it. Things don't just go in the weights right away. But if you see kind of every new generation of models, the models get better not because the prompt is better, but because they train them more. Training is useful. Training works. Training is why we see the progress we do. And the model is roughly like trained on lots of data that is aiming to approximate things that the labs expect will be like high value repeatable workflows at organizations. And I like this. I think there's a process that currently it works. It's how the models get better. But if you spell it out, it's relatively inefficient. So the way that a model would learn how to get really good at using some combination of, like, Salesforce tools, for example, let's say, is someone who knows how those tools get used has to be looking for work and maybe they previously worked at a place that were using these tools and now they are browsing kind of expert network sites to make some money in their free time. And they are sharing their knowledge to someone who works at an expert network company. This person at this network company will then take this data from the human and pass it to someone else whose job is to create RL environments. This RL environment might get sold then by someone who doesn't have this expert knowledge to a researcher at a lab who also really isn't an expert in the domain who then will be refining it to put it into a training pipeline to go into the next frontier model run to make a model that has kind of through this game of telephone gotten some knowledge of that human originally. But there's so many steps in this pipeline, and it's a relatively secret pipeline. People talk across two stages of it, but the human who knows this thing is not supervising the training run, is not really directly inputting how the model gets trained in the way that a human could if they were doing it for their coding agent that they're working with day to day. So what we see as an opportunity and kind of also where we would hope to go is to close this gap and to allow the person who the same way that when we work with our coding agents we're prompting them the same things every time telling them to not repeat the same mistakes. This is how you could train models. You can tell the models things, and they will learn these things durably. Not just as a line in your agent's MD which kind of accumulates and then you have to refactor it all the time. So you could do some of that, but a lot of times what you really want is you're giving kind of contextual preference. You're saying in this setting, this thing that you did was not exactly what I wanted and I would have preferred this instead. And we'd want systems that can compound this into, like, durable learning. And training is a very effective way of doing this because the shape of data you're giving there is quite close to what you would want from, like, an actual training pipeline. And so there's several different types of learning. There's things that people do. There's things that you can do at the harness layer with skills and memory. There's knowledge that just lives throughout an organization in file systems and databases that you retrieve with tools and with code. Then there's the models themselves which have this really broad world knowledge. But we all have, I'm sure, experienced frustration when using a model whose, like, cutoff of knowledge is, like, a while back and, like, you can't really talk to the models about the news of the past six months nowadays. They have to go, like, relearn a world model in context every single time. And this just does not allow them to really operate as fluently as they can discuss things that happened longer ago. And so organizations, to get the most value out of models, we imagine they will want to increasingly have models that really understand what is going on in the organization at an intuitive level. And this is the sort of thing that you want to train for. And so how do you get there? What is the road for an organization to go from, like, having this idea in the abstract of, like, we're going to train models on our data to actually getting there? And I think one really useful starting point is evals as essentially test cases. I think, like, with code, we've gotten to a point of maturity around, like, testing and life cycles and software development life cycles for ensuring that code bases grow healthily over time usually. And agents are doing so much of this work for us. And the version of continual learning that I think is, like, most practical for most organizations is just treating a model kind of like a code base, where it is the sort of thing that you can have a life cycle around. You can add test cases to. You can add features to. You can add assets to. And this is the sort of thing that the process of using agents, like, initially you collect traces. These traces have your prompts and they have your feedback to things that models did. And this just from the process of using these models, you are accumulating the assets you need to create evals. It's just that making evals historically has been a little bit painful and a lot of organizations have not necessarily wanted to do it manually. But the agents are quite quickly getting to the point where thankfully we have robots that can do a lot of the eval curation for us, especially as we train them more on the best practices of making evals in ways that are robust and amenable to learning. And so I think another useful example here is the decision model craze that has kind of been taking the world by storm in the past couple weeks with Jev and also the parallels around routing and people being very excited about cost optimization because we see that, like, it's possible to spend very large amounts of money on Cloud every month and we figure out, like, when should we use a cheaper model? And this is the sort of thing that I think people are recognizing needs to kind of live in the harness. But it also is an attribute that looks relatively similar to decision models. And the reason I bring both of these up together is because there's things with very clear labels where there's a right answer and there's an opportunity for a human or another agent to give feedback. You can have the big model and the small model do the same task, judge whether the small model was as good as the big model. If so, then this is now data of, like, for this kind of thing, we can start routing to the small model more. So if you're looking for a decision model that's learning to kind of mimic the way that a human in a certain situation would make a judgment, this is a great labelable action where the human might be doing the approval the same way that, like, we approve our tool calls in Cloud Code sometimes. But I think most people have turned on, like, auto tool acceptance. But every organization for more bespoke things that aren't just about, like, tool security are going to have their own rules and preferences. And these are the sorts of things that you could then compound into a decision model. And so this is, like, a very believable form of continual learning that a lot of people could just plug in tomorrow and see immediate value from. But more broadly what we see people wanting to do, and this is a lot of the work that we do at Prime Intellect, is working with organizations that are looking to do relatively ambitious training projects.
